Establish
es-tab'lish
v. (to make firm, to settle, to confirm; rendering Hebrew qum and kun, Greek histemi and sterizo)
From the Latin stabilio, to make stable, from sto, to stand, through Old French establir. The KJV also uses the older form stablish. Hebrew qum is to raise up and cause to stand; kun, to set firm.

Biblical Definition

To establish is to make a thing stand, and in Scripture the subject of the verb is almost always God. He establishes covenants: “And I, behold, I establish my covenant with you, and with your seed after you” (Genesis 9:9) — the pronoun is doubled for emphasis, and Noah is not asked to agree to terms. The covenant stands because God stands behind it, which is what distinguishes a biblical covenant from a contract between equals. Man's part is to ask for the establishing rather than to supply it: “establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it” (Psalm 90:17) — the request repeated in the same breath, by a man who has just spent a psalm on how briefly hands work at all. Proverbs gives the ordinary mechanism: “Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established” (Proverbs 16:3), where the committing is ours and the establishing is his, and the thing steadied is not the circumstances but the mind. And Paul uses the word at the hinge of his argument on justification: “Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law” (Romans 3:31). Justification by faith alone does not abolish the law; it is the only doctrine that ever honoured it, since in the cross the law's full penalty was paid rather than waived.

Webster 1828 Definition

To make firm; to cause to stand. God establishes his covenant unilaterally, Moses asks him to establish the work of our hands, and Paul says justification by faith establishes the law rather than voiding it.

expand to see more

ESTABLISH, v.t. [Fr. establir; L. stabilio, from sto, to stand.] To set and fix firmly or unalterably; to settle permanently.

2. To found permanently; to erect and fix or settle; as, to establish a colony or an empire.

3. To enact or decree by authority and for permanence; to ordain; to appoint; as, to establish laws.

4. To confirm; to fix or settle in opinion; as, to establish a man in the truth.

5. To make good; to prove and cause to be accepted as true; as, to establish a fact or a doctrine.

Key Scripture

Genesis 9:9 — "And I, behold, I establish my covenant with you, and with your seed after you;"

Psalm 90:17 — "And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it."

Deuteronomy 8:18 — "But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth, that he may establish his covenant which he sware unto thy fathers, as it is this day."

Proverbs 16:3 — "Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established."

Modern Corruption

Justification by faith is charged with making the law void — the antinomian error Paul answers with an emphatic God forbid — while men attempt to establish by effort what only God can settle.

expand to see more

Romans 3:31 answers a charge as old as the gospel: that a righteousness reckoned by faith apart from works of law leaves the law with no standing. Paul's reply is that the opposite is true. The law is established at Calvary precisely because it was not relaxed there — God did not lower the requirement, he satisfied it, so that he might be just and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus. Antinomianism, which treats grace as release from obligation, and legalism, which treats obedience as the ground of acceptance, both fail to see what the cross did to the law. The believer is not under the law as a covenant of works and remains under it as a rule of life, which is the ordinary Reformed distinction and the answer to both errors.

The principle to recover is the direction of the establishing. Psalm 90 is a psalm about brevity — we spend our years as a tale that is told, our days are threescore years and ten — and its last request is that God would make the work of such short-lived hands stand. Moses does not ask for longer life or larger work; he asks that what is done should last, and he asks twice. Every believer who has watched good work undone knows the prayer. Nothing a man builds outlives him unless God establishes it, and the request is one God delights to grant.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qum is to arise, to cause to stand, used of establishing a covenant; kun is to be firm or fixed. Greek histemi is to make stand; sterizo, to prop or strengthen.

expand to see more

Hebrew qum (H6965) — to rise, to raise up, to establish; the verb of establishing a covenant.

Hebrew kun (H3559) — to be firm, set upright, prepared; established thoughts and an established throne.

Greek histemi (G2476) — to make to stand; we establish the law, Romans 3:31.

Greek sterizo (G4741) — to set fast, to strengthen, to stablish; the Lord shall stablish you.

Greek bebaioo (G950) — to confirm, make sure; God stablisheth us with you in Christ.

Usage

"Of a covenant God establishes alone: I establish my covenant with you (Genesis 9:9)."

"Of the prayer for lasting work: establish thou the work of our hands upon us (Psalm 90:17)."

"Of faith upholding the law: yea, we establish the law (Romans 3:31)."
